qs.q: A patient receiving total parenteral nutrition develops dermatitis, alopecia, and neurological abnormalities. Analysis reveals a deficiency in a crucial cofactor for carboxylation reactions. Which enzyme is affected?
o: Superoxide dismutase neutralizing reactive oxygen compounds
Glycogen phosphorylase releasing glucose from hepatic storage
Carbonic anhydrase maintaining systemic acid-base equilibrium
Pyruvate carboxylase functioning within gluconeogenesis pathways
Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase initiating heme biosynthesis
qs.e: Biotin is the essential prosthetic group for carboxylases like pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and propionyl-CoA carboxylase.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Clinical Biochemistry Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient undergoing total parenteral nutrition develops dry skin, hair loss, and impaired vision in dim light. Which specific fat-soluble vitamin deficiency matches these ocular and integumentary signs?
qs.e: Vitamin A (retinol) is crucial for epithelial maintenance and rhodopsin formation in retinal rod cells.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Nutrition and Dietetics Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with an enterocutaneous fistula demonstrates persistent tachycardia, spiking fevers, and failure to progress towards fistula closure despite two weeks of total parenteral nutrition and fluid resuscitation. What is the most critical factor preventing spontaneous closure in this patient?
qs.e: Spontaneous closure cannot occur in the presence of sepsis, making its control the most important determinant of outcome. While nutrition is vital, it cannot overcome active uncontrolled infection.
qs.s: Intestinal and Enterocutaneous Fistulas: Classification and Management: MCQs

qs.q: An infant receiving total parenteral nutrition and broad-spectrum antibiotics for stage II necrotising enterocolitis develops direct hyperbilirubinaemia and conjugated jaundice. Which aspect of the ongoing management plan is the direct cause of bowel rest?
o: Maintain nil per os for seven to fourteen days
Place an orogastric tube with low intermittent suction
Perform serial abdominal examinations every four hours
qs.e: Bowel rest is achieved by stopping all enteral feeds (nil by mouth) for 7 to 14 days. Gastric decompression uses an orogastric or nasogastric tube, but the cessation of feeds is the defining feature of bowel rest.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old male patient with a high-output proximal enterocutaneous fistula requires complete nutritional replacement. Which statement best justifies the choice of total parenteral nutrition for this patient?
o: Parenteral nutrition completely avoids all infectious complications
The gut is fully functioning and capable of absorbing macronutrients
PPN can safely provide long-term high caloric intake without issues
The patient has abnormal gut function and cannot absorb nutrients
qs.e: High-output proximal enterocutaneous fistulas cause abnormal gut function where nutrients cannot be absorbed, making TPN the required modality. PPN is restricted to short-term use.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old man is being prepared for total parenteral nutrition. Before starting the infusion, what initial clinical and laboratory preparation must be prioritized?
o: Correction of dehydration, electrolyte, and acid-base disorders
Discontinuation of all baseline liver function and coagulation
Routine administration of oral supplements to test absorption
Immediate insertion of a peripheral IV line for lipid-free feeds
qs.e: Dehydration, electrolyte, and acid-base disorders must be corrected first before starting TPN to prevent fatal shifts and metabolic instability. Baseline bloods and vascular access assessment are also required.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

qs.q: A 48-year-old man on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) develops recurrent fever and chills on day 7. The central venous catheter site appears normal. What is the most likely cause of this complication?
qs.e: Catheter sepsis is recognized as the commonest serious problem associated with total parenteral nutrition. Air embolism and refeeding syndrome present differently or earlier in the course of therapy.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with intestinal failure is started on total parenteral nutrition. Her daily prescription includes standard multivitamin ampoules. Which specific vitamin must be supplemented separately because it is absent from standard multivitamins?
qs.e: Standard multivitamin preparations do not include vitamin K, which must be given separately at 1 mg a day or 5 to 10 mg a week. Vitamin B12 and folate are included in the standard supplement.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

es.q: Discuss the indications and baseline requirements before starting Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN).
es.m:
- **Indications for use:** Reserved for patients with abnormal gut function, inability to consume adequate amounts enterally, an anticipated inability to eat for more than 5 to 7 days, or when the prognosis warrants aggressive support.
- **Pre-TPN assessment:** Requires a nutritional assessment, assessment of venous access via a dedicated central line with a fast flow, and a baseline weight.
- **Baseline laboratory tests:** Must include a full blood count, coagulation screen, urea and electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, liver function tests, glucose, and lipid profile.
- **Correction of imbalances:** Dehydration, electrolyte disorders, and acid-base disorders must be corrected first
es.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: Essay questio

ai.title: Total Parenteral Nutrition
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: TPN delivers all nutrients intravenously when the gut cannot be used. It requires central access, careful monitoring of electrolytes, glucose and lipids, and prevention of line‑related infections.

sections.p: TPN is a complete nutrition solution given through a central venous line when enteral feeding is impossible or contraindicated. Diagnosis is clinical: inability to meet caloric needs orally or enterally for >5–7 days.

Severity is staged by duration and complications: short‑term (≤2 weeks) vs long‑term (>2 weeks). Complications such as catheter sepsis, metabolic derangements or liver dysfunction define advanced stages.
Common causes in low‑resource settings include bowel obstruction, severe pancreatitis, short bowel syndrome, postoperative ileus, and severe infections that preclude oral intake.
Patients appear well‑nourished but have no oral intake, abdominal distension, or signs of ileus. Labs show hyperglycaemia, electrolyte shifts, and rising liver enzymes.
Baseline and ongoing labs guide composition and detect complications.

t.b: Assess sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium – abnormal levels indicate need for adjustment
Monitor for hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia – guides dextrose infusion
Elevated transaminases or bilirubin suggest cholestasis or fatty liver
INR, aPTT to detect vitamin K deficiency or liver dysfunction
If fever or catheter site redness – indicates catheter‑related sepsis

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden fever, chills, catheter site erythema, worsening abdominal pain, or metabolic acidosis. Complications: catheter sepsis, line thrombosis, hyperglycaemia, refeeding syndrome, liver dysfunction, and lipid emboli.

Treat underlying cause, insert a central line, start a balanced TPN solution (carbohydrate, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins). Monitor labs daily, adjust composition, and prevent infection with aseptic technique.

t.b: If catheter sepsis – broad‑spectrum covering gram‑positive and gram‑negative organisms; avoid nephrotoxic agents
If INR >1.5 – to prevent bleeding complications

sections.p: Regular review of nutritional status, line integrity, and metabolic parameters. Early transition to enteral feeding when feasible reduces infection risk.

t.b: Assess tolerance and caloric uptake – indicates readiness to stop TPN

sections.p: Parenteral nutrition (PN) without total calories, or enteral feeding via nasogastric tube. Also confused with refeeding syndrome – a metabolic complication of rapid nutrition restart.
Low serum albumin may be normal in TPN patients due to lack of protein synthesis; normal glucose may mask hyperglycaemia if dextrose is not monitored closely.
b: Albumin low but not indicative of malnutrition
Glucose may appear normal if not checked frequently

faq.q: What is the minimum duration of TPN before considering complications?
faq.a: Complications may arise after 2–3 weeks of continuous TPN, especially catheter sepsis and liver dysfunction.

faq.q: Why are lipids given in a separate infusion?
faq.a: Lipids are concentrated; giving them separately prevents hypertriglyceridaemia and allows better control of caloric intake.

faq.q: Can a patient on TPN develop refeeding syndrome?
faq.a: Yes, especially if they are severely malnourished; monitor electrolytes and give thiamine before starting nutrition.

exam: A 30‑year‑old woman with severe pancreatitis is not tolerating enteral feeds. What is the first step in initiating TPN? — Insert a central venous catheter, start a balanced TPN solution, and monitor electrolytes and glucose.

A patient on TPN develops fever and catheter site erythema. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — Catheter‑related sepsis; obtain blood cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and consider catheter removal.

A TPN patient shows rising transaminases and bilirubin. What does this indicate and how should you adjust therapy? — Early liver dysfunction; reduce lipid infusion rate and consider adding ursodeoxycholic acid.
A child on TPN has hypophosphatemia and muscle weakness. What syndrome is this and what is the treatment? — Refeeding syndrome; give phosphate supplements and thiamine.
A patient on TPN has hyperglycaemia despite insulin infusion. What adjustment is needed? — Increase insulin dose or reduce dextrose concentration in the TPN solution.
A TPN line is clogged after 4 weeks. What is the most appropriate action? — Flush with heparinised saline, reassess line patency, and consider line change if infection suspected.

A patient on TPN develops sudden abdominal pain and distension. What is the differential and first investigation? — Possible bowel perforation or obstruction; obtain an abdominal X‑ray and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
